title: Why are min/max statistics and dictionary filtering ineffective for high-cardinality unsorted columns (wide min/max range, huge dictionaries), and how do bloom filters help (compact bitset, "definitely not present" → skip, "probably present" → read)?
shortTitle: Why min/max and dictionary filtering fail on high-cardinality unsorted columns, and how bloom filters help

s1_definition.profdef: Min/max statistics fail on high-cardinality unsorted columns because every block ends up containing values spanning almost the entire domain, so each block's min/max range overlaps the filter value and nothing can be skipped. Dictionary filtering fails because a high-cardinality column has so many distinct values that either the dictionary grows too large to be efficient or Parquet abandons dictionary encoding altogether, removing the membership check. Bloom filters solve this by storing a small fixed-size bitset per block built by hashing each value; testing a value gives "definitely not present," which allows a safe skip, or "probably present," which forces a read, giving effective skipping even for billions of distinct unsorted values.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose the National Bank of India fills archive boxes randomly with records from every account. The label "smallest and largest account id in this box" becomes meaningless because every box, filled randomly, spans from the first account to the last — so when you look for one account, no box can be ruled out. Listing every account id in the box (dictionary) is hopeless when a box holds millions of distinct ids. A bloom filter is a tiny fingerprint card on each box: you scan your account's fingerprint against it and it can firmly say "not in this box," letting you skip, even though the box holds millions of ids.
s1_definition.oneliner: On high-cardinality unsorted columns, min/max ranges span everything and dictionaries explode, so only a bloom filter's "definitely not present" answer lets Parquet skip blocks.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Min/max statistics fail on high-cardinality unsorted columns because every block ends up containing values spanning almost the entire domain, so each block's min/max range overlaps the filter value and nothing can be skipped. Dictionary filtering fails because a high-cardinality column has so many distinct values that either the dictionary grows too large to be efficient or Parquet abandons dictionary encoding altogether, removing the membership check. Bloom filters solve this by storing a small fixed-size bitset per block built by hashing each value; testing a value gives "definitely not present," which allows a safe skip, or "probably present," which forces a read, giving effective skipping even for billions of distinct unsorted values.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose the National Bank of India fills archive boxes randomly with records from every account. The label "smallest and largest account id in this box" becomes meaningless because every box, filled randomly, spans from the first account to the last — so when you look for one account, no box can be ruled out. Listing every account id in the box (dictionary) is hopeless when a box holds millions of distinct ids. A bloom filter is a tiny fingerprint card on each box: you scan your account's fingerprint against it and it can firmly say "not in this box," letting you skip, even though the box holds millions of ids.

**One line to remember:** On high-cardinality unsorted columns, min/max ranges span everything and dictionaries explode, so only a bloom filter's "definitely not present" answer lets Parquet skip blocks.

sections.s2_technical:
Min/max statistics work by recording the smallest and largest value in each block. Their power comes from tight, mostly non-overlapping ranges, which you only get when the data is sorted on that column. For a high-cardinality column that is unsorted — say a random transaction id or a hashed account id scattered across the file — each block receives a random sample of the whole value space. As a result, almost every block's minimum is near the global minimum and its maximum near the global maximum. When you filter for one specific id, that id falls inside nearly every block's range, so the reader cannot prove any block is safe to skip. The statistics are present and correct, but they prune nothing.

Dictionary filtering works by checking whether an equality value exists in a block's dictionary of distinct values. It is effective when the column has few distinct values, because the dictionary is small and the membership check is cheap and selective. For a high-cardinality column, two things go wrong. First, the dictionary becomes huge, consuming space and reducing the compression benefit. Second, Parquet has a dictionary size threshold, and once a column's distinct values in a block exceed it, Parquet falls back to plain encoding and drops the dictionary, so there is no dictionary page to check. Either way, dictionary filtering stops helping for high-cardinality columns.

Bloom filters are the purpose-built answer. A bloom filter is a fixed-size array of bits. When writing, each value is hashed by several hash functions, and the corresponding bits are set. When reading, to test whether a value could be present, you hash it the same way and check those bits. If any required bit is zero, the value was never inserted, so it is definitely not present and the block is safely skipped. If all bits are set, the value is probably present — it might be a false positive from other values setting the same bits — so the block must be read. The key properties are that bloom filters never give false negatives, which makes skipping safe, and they are compact, using a few bits per value regardless of the value's size. This lets a small structure represent membership for millions of distinct ids.

A senior-level nuance is the cost and configuration. Bloom filters are not free: they add bytes to the file and are not built by default, so you enable them per column at write time only for high-cardinality columns you filter by equality, such as transaction id or customer id. The false-positive rate is tunable by sizing the bitset and choosing the number of hash functions; a larger filter means fewer false positives but more storage. Bloom filters only help equality and IN predicates, not ranges, because hashing destroys order. And the complementary strategy is to sort or Z-order on the column instead, which fixes min/max, but you cannot sort by many columns at once, so bloom filters cover the high-cardinality equality lookups that sorting cannot.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores billions of transactions and frequently looks up a single transaction id. Transaction id is extremely high cardinality and the data is sorted by date, not id, so id min/max in every block spans nearly the whole id space and skips nothing. This is the min/max failure.

Problem 2 — The id column has millions of distinct values per block, so Parquet dropped dictionary encoding for it, meaning there is no dictionary page to consult. This is the dictionary failure.

Problem 3 — Enabling a bloom filter on transaction id lets each block answer definitely-not-present for the looked-up id, so the reader skips the vast majority of blocks and reads only the one that probably contains it. This is the bloom filter rescue.

The demo models blocks for a high-cardinality unsorted id column, shows that min/max cannot skip and the dictionary is absent, then applies a bloom filter and reports the dramatic reduction in blocks read.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/spark-bloom-lookup-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.spark.BloomLookupDemo

# In a real Spark job — enable a bloom filter on the high-card lookup column:
#   txns.write
#       .option("parquet.bloom.filter.enabled#txnId", "true")
#       .option("parquet.bloom.filter.expected.ndv#txnId", "100000000")
#       .parquet("s3://bank/txns")
#   # point lookups then skip most blocks:
#   spark.read.parquet("s3://bank/txns").filter(col("txnId") === "TX-424242")
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four Parquet blocks of unsorted high-cardinality transaction ids; a lookup for TX-424242, which lives only in block 2.

Step 1: The reader tries min/max. Because the ids are unsorted, every block holds ids from near the start to near the end of the id space, so every block's min-to-max range contains TX-424242. No block can be ruled out, so min/max skips nothing.

Step 2: The reader tries dictionary filtering. The id column has far too many distinct values, so Parquet dropped dictionary encoding for it, which means there is no dictionary page to consult. Dictionary filtering gives no help.

Step 3: The reader uses the bloom filter. For each block it hashes TX-424242 and checks the bits. Blocks 0, 1, and 3 have at least one required bit clear, so they return definitely-not-present and are skipped. Block 2 has all bits set, so it returns probably-present and is read.

Step 4: The demo reports that only one of four blocks is read for the point lookup, a result neither min/max nor dictionary could achieve on this column.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  High-cardinality UNSORTED txnId, lookup TX-424242
    │
    ├─ min/max:  every block [min..max] ⊇ lookup  → 0 skips
    │
    ├─ dictionary: too many distinct ids → encoding dropped → no page
    │
    ▼ bloom filter (compact bitset per block)
       hash(lookup) → check bits
         any bit 0 → DEFINITELY NOT PRESENT → SKIP   (B0, B1, B3)
         all bits 1 → PROBABLY PRESENT      → READ   (B2)
       result: read 1 of 4 blocks
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Min/max statistics and dictionary filtering both break down on high-cardinality unsorted columns, and bloom filters are the fix. Min/max records the smallest and largest value per block, and it only prunes when those ranges are tight and non-overlapping, which requires the data to be sorted on that column. For a high-cardinality column that is unsorted, each block receives a random spread of values, so nearly every block's minimum is close to the global minimum and its maximum close to the global maximum. When I look up one specific value it falls inside almost every block's range, so no block can be ruled out and min/max skips nothing.

Dictionary filtering checks whether the value exists in a block's dictionary of distinct values, which is cheap and selective when there are few distinct values. But a high-cardinality column has so many distinct values that the dictionary either grows too large to help or exceeds Parquet's dictionary threshold, at which point Parquet drops dictionary encoding entirely and there is no dictionary page left to consult. So dictionary filtering also stops working.

Bloom filters are built exactly for this case. A bloom filter is a small fixed-size bitset per block; at write time each value is hashed by several functions and the corresponding bits are set. At read time I hash the lookup value and check those bits — if any is clear, the value was never inserted, so it is definitely not present and the block is safely skipped, and if all are set it is probably present and must be read. The two properties that matter are that bloom filters never produce false negatives, which makes skipping safe, and that they are compact, using a few bits per value, so a tiny structure represents membership for millions of ids. At the National Bank of India our transaction table was sorted by date, so date filters used min/max, but point lookups by transaction id — extremely high cardinality and not the sort key — skipped nothing until we enabled bloom filters on the id column, after which a lookup read just the one block that probably contained it. The rule I give is that bloom filters cost space and are off by default, so you enable them per column only for high-cardinality equality lookups, and they help equality and IN predicates, not ranges.
